text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--The three-year old central public buying authority, The State and Local Authority Purchasing Service, bought 2.3 billion crowns worth of goods and services in 1996, one billion more than in 1994, its first year of operation.

--Danish industrial workers' wages are on average rising less than consumer prices but still more than in competing economies such as Germany. Danish employers are asking the government to ease taxes in order to protect workers' purchasing power while improving export competitiveness.

--The Danish Bankers' Association is expected today to approve new guidlines from the consumer council for ethics in banking. At the heart of the new rules is that investment advice must be made in the customer's best interest, rather than the banks'.
--Justice Minister Frank Jensen is seeking to have unpaid fines retrieved directly from miscreants' salaries. More than 11,000 people were jailed last year for non-payment of fines.
--A survey of Denmark's top businesses shows that those who are widely diversified are the most profitable, rather than those who concentrate on limited core activities.

--Politicians from both the opposition and Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen's Social Democrats are accusing him of trying to scare voters into backing the Amsterdam EU treaty by focusing on the potential harm to Denmark of a 'no' vote in a referendum expected early next year.

--It is public spending rather than private consumption which is growing too fast and moves to cut the latter could have negative consequences, Den Danske Bank Chief Economist Joergen Birger Christensen says. REUTERS
